title: ‘Halima,’ First Finnish Pic Ever by Black Female Filmmaker, Bags Fiction Project Prize, ‘Sauna Diplomacy’ Named Best Genre Project at Finnish Film Affair
description: Former BBC journalist Naima Mohamud’s heartfelt and warm comedy “Halima,” about a 10-year-old Somali girl trying to fit in Finland in 1998 took home
body:
Former BBC journalist Naima Mohamud’s heartfelt and warm comedy “Halima,” about a 10-year-old Somali girl trying to fit in Finland in 1998 took home Helsinki’s Finnish Film Affair’s top prize for Best Fiction on Thursday evening.

	The award was handed out by the jury, including U.S. producer and executive Jodi Hildebrand (formerly at Condé Nast and Marvel Studios), the British Film Institute’s Phoebe Hall and FEST-New Directors festival director Fernando Vasquez, who said: “The director’s energetic and authentic voice shone through in the pitch and translates into what promises to be a compelling lead performance. This is a 90s tinged snapshot of a Finland we haven’t seen on screen before, by a fresh Finnish voice.”
	



	

					“11 Hours”
									Courtesy of Fenomen
	



	Produced by It’s Alive Films (“Euthanizer,” “The Man Who Did Not Want to See Titanic,” “100 Litres of Gold”), Finland’s regular provider of artistically daring and original scripted content, Mohamud’s debut feature marks a milestone as the very first Finnish feature film directed by a black woman. “But it’s also the first film not directed by Teemo [Nikki], co-owner of the company,” said It’s Alive’s co-founder and producer Jani Pösö at his pitch, while reminding the 500-plus delegates that their films are “entertaining takes on deadly serious subjects.”


	“This is the same here, and we simply had to make this movie,” added Pösö, who produces with Finland’s No-Office Films, in co-production with Ireland’s Vico Films.

	“This story was inspired by my family, and my experience of growing up in Finland, where no one had seen black people!” said Dublin and Helsinki-based Mohamud, who studied filmmaking at London Metropolitan University and USC (University of Southern California) in Los Angeles. The feature, which won Best Pitch at the Haugesund New Nordic Films in 2024, is now in post-production with a delivery set for the fall 2027.
	

	At Thursday’s awards ceremony, which closed the showcase day at Helsinki Film Festival’s industry confab Finnish Film Affair, the jury also handed out the €3,000 ($3,400) Best Nordic Film Award from the Amos Anderson Fund to the Norwegian suspense drama “11 Hours” by Emilie Beck, best-known for Netflix’s “Royalteen” and TV2 Norway’s hit “Escaping Bolivia.”

	Inspired by true events, the pic chronicles the traumatic 11 hours that daycare director Sara, her employees and 11 children had to endure when an armed man took them hostage.

	“This pitch made us all immediately lean forward in our seats,” said the jury. “Using the form of a ripped-from-the-headlines hostage thriller to illuminate a complex and layered social story, it’s a film we can’t wait to see more of.”

	Toplining an A-list Norwegian cast including Ingrid Bolsø Berdal (“La Palma,” “Detective Hole”), Jan Gunnar Røise (Dag Johan Haugerud’s “Sex”), Oddgeir Thune (“Loveable,” “Home for Christmas”) and Sofia Tjelta (“Delete Me”), the feature, produced by Fenomen Studios and Maha Film, will be released domestically in September 2027 via Scanbox.

	In other main categories, the new €2,500 ($2,800) Best Genre Project, sponsored by Post Control Helsinki & Angel Films, crowned Teenu Niukkanen’s “Sauna Diplomacy,” the only comedy among eight projects that competed in the high-profile inaugural Nordic Genre Lab.

	“We believe that the project was a clear stand out,” said jury members Noëmie Devide (Goodfellas), Sydney Brumfield (Searchlight) and screenwriter Espen Auka, who felt the concept was “very original, fun and commercially viable.”

	Set in the summer of 1970, the story turns on the diligent civil servant Heikki who decides to host a high-ranking Soviet diplomat at his family’s lakeside cottage. But the seemingly harmless weekend turns into a game of manipulation, and power games.

	“It’s set during Finlandization, when Finland during the Cold War was a pre-western democracy, as long as the Soviet Union would tell us what to do!,” quipped Niukkanen (“Fucking Bunnies,” “Money Shot”), a self-proclaimed creator of content with “bad taste, done with good taste.”

	“I recommend reading Teemu’s script! It’s fuckingly funny – topical, rowdy, thrillingly violent, yet a much-needed guide on how to stand up against tyrants,” said Oskari Huttu, who produces with John Lundsten for Tack Films. The project in development has been pre-bought by Nordisk Film for the Nordics, with production set to kickstart in 2028.
	

	Elsewhere, the €3,000 AVEK Best Documentary Award handed out by IDFA’s Isabel Arrate Fernandez, director Einari Paakkanen and the Estonian Film Institute’s doc specialist Filipp Kruusvall, went to Anna Antsalo (“Walk the Tideline”) for her film “Darkness Counts,” produced by Venla Hellstedt.

	“The award for best documentary project goes to a project that turns the greatest enemy of filmmaking – darkness – into a visually captivating element,” said the jury.

	Reflecting the Finnish Film Affair’s ever-expanding collaborations with key European markets to facilitate networking and business opportunities for Finnish and Nordic professionals, an extra four industry awards were given out on Thursday.


In a tightly fought series competition, the six-part comedy thriller “Body in the Closet” from “Bloodsuckers’” Elin Grönblom grabbed the Midpoint Series Consulting Award. The series produced by Mia Oikanen for Warner Bros Int’l Television Production Finland tells of a shy theater prop master who accidentally becomes a killer while trying to please everyone around her, especially her narcissistic mom. “Yes, there are murders, but no one cares about the murderer and murdered people – they only care about themselves!” said MFA graduate Grönblom in her entertaining pitch.
The Midpoint Institute also granted its Feature Consulting Award to the courtroom drama in development “Big Deal,” helmed by Hedda Mjøn for Oda Kruse, in which four character’s lives are irrevocably changed by a single trial. SF Studios has boarded the Norwegian, Finnish, Estonian co-production.
The inaugural Producers Network Award from the Marché du Film went to the Finnish project in development “Babyface” by Aleksi Delikouras (“Nerd:DragonSlayer666”), a modern-day “Karate Kid” in which a 13-year-old boy befriends the eccentric pro wrestler Killer Joe. “I want to offer a different image of masculinity, and show that vulnerability is not a weakness,” said Delikouras in his pitch.
Finally It’s Alive Films’ psycho horror “Linden Lane 6” from rising talent Josefina Rautiainen picked up the Göteborg Film Festival Award. The story focuses on a novelist who moves into a building, strangely inhabited only by woman – 13 of them. The project in development is being produced by Anita Hyppönen, recipient as well of the Connecting Cottbus Producers Exchange accolade.



	Commenting on the overall industry event, Searchlight’s Sydney Brumfield, who was in Helsinki for her Nordic Genre Lab duty, said Finnish Film Affair organizers “did an excellent job in selecting the projects because the quality was amazing.”

	Her views were shared by Tonje Hardersen, head of the Norwegian Int’l Film Festival. “It’s been a very strong year and many projects stood out,” said the seasoned Norwegian executive, who had Emilie Beck’s “11 Hours” in her list of top projects.

schema.headline: ‘Halima,’ First Finnish Pic Ever by Black Female Filmmaker, Bags Fiction Project Prize, ‘Sauna Diplomacy’ Named Best Genre Project at Finnish Film Affair

title: ‘Florid’ Director Billy Lumby on Challenging ‘Misrepresentation’ of Schizophrenia on Screen and Casting Non-Actors in Feature Debut
description: The depiction of schizophrenia on screen — especially in horror movies — has largely seen the mental health condition linked to violent and unpredic
body:
The depiction of schizophrenia on screen — especially in horror movies — has largely seen the mental health condition linked to violent and unpredictable rages, showing people when something has gone horribly wrong. 

	This “misrepresentation,” according to British filmmaker Billy Lumby (a BAFTA nominee for his short film “Samuel-613”), was part of the inspiration behind his feature directorial debut “Florid,” having its world premiere at San Sebastian Film Festival.
	

	The film — also borne out of Lumby’s own mental health experiences — follows Jamal, a young man who hears voices (Lumby says he prefers this term to “schizophrenia”) and is struggling to balance the medication he’s supposed to be taking with his marijuana consumption. Living in supported housing in East London alongside others with mental health issues, Jamal finds himself increasingly lonely and isolated, with the voices in his head, one relating to past family events, only intensifying once he decides to throw his pills away.


	While the story doesn’t culminate in the violent depths seen in the cinema tropes Lumby was purposefully looking to avoid, it’s a tough watch. But that’s largely due to the aural sensation provided by the voices, which become more powerful and prominent as the film progresses, dragging Jamal down with them.

	Carrying “Florid” as Jamal is Jonathan Jules, best known for Steve McQueen’s “Small Axe,” in his first lead role. “It’s not easy to act in a mentally unwell state in an authentic, accurate way,” notes Lumby.

	During filming, Jules wore earpieces on set, with actors in another room speaking into microphones so he could hear the voices live and respond in an unrestricted way. “There were theses little moments where his eyes twitched — it just made if feel so real,” says Lumby. After principal photography wrapped, many months would be spent in post-production augmenting the voices to create the right tone and weave them into the overall soundscape.
	

	Making the editing process even more complex was the fact that Jamal hears three voices. There’s a little girl, representing his self-worth and highly critical of him. Then there’s the voice of real-life rapper Unknown T, who hypes him up. “That’s his more grandiose side, building up his ego and making him think that big things are going on in his life,” says Lumby. But most destructive is the voice of Jamal’s stepdad, which is a negative, paranoid voice that tries to convince him to doubt the intentions of those around him.

	“When he’s well, he can ignore these things and it’s just like a little anxious thought in the background,” says Lumby, who was heavily inspired by the Hearing Voices Movement, which rejects traditional psychiatric notions that such voices are merely hallucinations to be dulled through medication. Instead, it argues that they can be a valid part of someone’s identity and history and don’t always exist as a negative experience.



	

					Jamal Jules in ‘Florid’
	



	While Lumby says there are definite “autobiographical elements” to “Florid,” he went to great lengths to achieve additional authenticity. As part of years of research into the U.K.’s National Health Service and its mental health system, he went on psychiatric wards across London, shadowed social workers and met those with mental health experiences, plus their families and carers. Lead actor Jules spent time in the NHS, as his co-star Saskia Chana, who plays another resident of the supported housing and potential love interest. But many of the other roles went to non-actors that Lumby met during the extensive development process.

	“We have real psychiatrists, social workers, real people with lived experiences, people with diagnoses of schizophrenia, bipolar and severe mental health experiences,” he says. Jamal’s care coordinator is played by Claire Holman, an real NHS care coordinator and someone Lumby says “opened a lot of doors” in the mental health community for him.

	Lumby asserts that Holman and the others from the mental health community wanted to be involved in the project because, like him, they were “passionate” about the subject matter and also “haven’t seen it represented properly or seen their lives shown before.”

	The main purpose of “Florid,” which is produced by Rupert Lloyd (an Oscar nominee for “Theeb”) and Joy Gharoro-Akpojotor (“Blue Story,” “Boxing Day”), is “awareness,” says Lumby. 
	

	“I wanted to draw attention to an area of our world and our modern contemporary society that many people are not aware of,” he says, adding that mental health is the “least funded” area of the NHS. 

	“There’s a lot of stigmatization and misrepresentation, and I think the more that we open up and discuss these things, the better. Not everyone may not like my film, but hopefully it causes some kind of discussion and debate around severe mental health. People talk about depression and anxiety, but in the case of severe mental health, I think it’s something that’s still not fully understood.”

title: ‘Unabomber’ Review: A Portrait of the Terrorist as a Young Man, Given a Hokey TV-Movie Gloss
description: The Unabomber may be a figure of enduring public fascination, but it’s hard to see that extending to “Unabomber,” Netflix‘s unimaginatively titled a
body:
The Unabomber may be a figure of enduring public fascination, but it’s hard to see that extending to “Unabomber,” Netflix‘s unimaginatively titled and prosaically assembled drama about how domestic terrorist Ted Kaczynski was radicalized, and how he was caught. Alternating between a standard-issue procedural thriller, dramatizing the FBI’s final year of investigation on the case, and psychologically revealing flashbacks to the 16-year-old Kaczynski’s freshman year at Harvard, Janus Metz‘s film has some built-in intrigue from its subject matter alone, but rote dialogue and autopilot true-crime styling do little to fire the imagination. Meanwhile, the dual timelines never spur or inform each other in any meaningful way; the sense that two disparate but half-baked Unabomber projects have been unhappily welded together is hard to shake.
	

	The more interesting of the two is the college-set narrative, which meets the streamer’s seemingly insatiable appetite for making-of-a-murderer biopics — call them true-life villain origin stories, if you will — and serves up a novel casting coup: Jacob Tremblay, the guileless child star of “Room” and “Wonder,” as the teenage Kaczynski. Portrayed as a butter-wouldn’t-melt prodigy unprepared to function in the real adult world, he’s pitted against Harvard professor Henry Murray, whose avuncular approach masks more manipulative intent as he enlists the vulnerable student as a subject in an experimental psychological study. 


	Played by Russell Crowe, who cruises through the film while remaining its most compelling figure, Murray is presented in Sam Chalsen and Nelson Greaves’ script as the unwitting architect of Kaczynski’s psychosis — and the spur behind his repeated targeting of academic figures with his bombings. Yet the film’s own case is pretty tenuous, and does little to counter Kaczynski’s later assertion that the experience, while unpleasant, wasn’t formative. Still, there’s more going on here than in the film’s 1990s-set section, which lumps Shailene Woodley with the stock role of fictional FBI agent Joanne Miller, battling institutional sexism and investigative complacency as she rather conveniently pieces together the Unabomber puzzle all on her own.
	

	There’s certainly little in the film to match the intensity of Tony Stone’s underseen 2021 biopic “Ted K,” starring a genuinely disquieting Sharlto Copley in the title role, which worked precisely because it didn’t try to crack or psychologize Kaczynski in the ways that “Unabomber” does to increasingly banal effect. While Miller pores over Kaczynski’s famous manifesto, correctly concluding that its linguistic quirks will lead the authorities to him, the upshot of Murray’s study four decades before is that the young Kaczynski shows signs of schizophrenia. Neither qualifies as a eureka moment likely to make slumping viewers sit bolt upright on their couch.

	The most complex story wrinkle here is the fact that Murray’s study, heavily rooted in his contentious “personology” theory of personality, is so patently unethical and specious — recruiting the young Kaczynski, among others, to debate his personal philosophies against a purposely combative and abusive opponent, solely for the purpose of observing how the hapless subject collapses under stress. Administered by Murray with his research partner Christiana Morgan (Annabelle Wallis), it’s written as a dastardly setup that serves to place Kaczynski in the most sympathetic possible light — while also showing the roots of his disconnect from society.

	As such, Kaczynski is characterized as little more than a twitchy grab-bag of symptoms, played by Tremblay with a fractured little-boy-lost affect that is never altogether convincing. When most under pressure, the performance retreats into a slightly one-note register of antisocial stridency — not that the hokey script, with all its heavily underlined tells and forced connections, calls for anything more finely shaded. Meanwhile, over at the FBI, Miller has the obtuse skepticism of her boorish partner Leo (a thankless role for Alexander Ludwig) to contend with while drawing perfectly logical conclusions from the evidence at hand; we vaguely feel for her, while also suspecting that the case can’t have been quite so simple.

	Metz, the Danish director of “Borg vs. McEnroe” and “All the Old Knives,” directs “Unabomber” in workaday style — beginning with a wholly unnecessary reenactment of the 1994 bombing that killed New Jersey ad exec Thomas J. Mosser (Michael Buie), which cues an archival recap of Kaczynski’s misdeeds for the benefit of anyone tuning in who might be unfamiliar. It’s an intro straight out of the Netflix true-crime playbook, which the film glossily follows throughout, while never seeming all that true. There’s little understanding to be gained from “Unabomber,” or even much tension from its fictionalized rejigging of the case — just the lurid draw of what we already know.

schema.headline: ‘Unabomber’ Review: A Portrait of the Terrorist as a Young Man, Given a Hokey TV-Movie Gloss

title: Silver Lion Winner ‘Miss Violence’ Director Alexandros Avranas to Helm Greek Adaptation of Globoplay’s Hit Series ‘The Others’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Alexandros Avranas, who won the Venice Film Festival Silver Lion for best director for the harrowing drama “Miss Violence,” will helm the Greek adap
body:
Alexandros Avranas, who won the Venice Film Festival Silver Lion for best director for the harrowing drama “Miss Violence,” will helm the Greek adaptation of Globoplay’s hit series “The Others.” The project, which is currently in production, follows the format sales agreement signed between Alpha TV and Brazilian media powerhouse Globo in late 2024.

	Created and written by top Brazilian TV creatve driving force  Lucas Paraizo, “The Others” follows two neighboring couples who clash after a fight between their teenage sons, triggering an escalating conflict with absurd consequences. What begins as a trivial disagreement reaches new proportions regarding how far a lack of dialogue can drive people. 
	

	The series is one of the most successful Globoplay original series to date, following in the footsteps of Paraizo’s hit medical drama “Under Pressure,” which was sold to more than 60 countries. In Brazil, the success of the franchise was consolidated with the premiere of its third season this year.




	

					Nikos Psarras (Petros) – Paschalis Terzis (Ektoras) – Marina Kalogirou (Melina)
	



	The Greek adaptation of the series is produced by Primavisione and stars Maria Nafpliotou (“Café 404”), Charis Fragulis (“Afterlov”), Nikos Psarras (“The Fire Bracelet”), and Paschalis Terzis. In addition to “The Others,” Greece will also get a local adaptation of the telenovela “All The Flowers,” with the same production company and broadcasting channel.



	

					Charis Fragkoulis (Alexandros) – Maria Nafpliotou (Sophia) – Sotiris Gkoros (Manos)
	



	To follow the start of production, author Lucas Paraizo visited the set in Greece: “I was on the set of the Greek version of ‘The Others’, a series I created, and had the pleasure of watching the shooting of one of the most important scenes of the first season: the scene where the characters Cibele and Wando face off over their sons’ fight,” he said.
	

	“I had the pleasure of witnessing the enthusiasm of the cast, crew, and director Alexandro Avranas, whom I’ve been a fan of since he directed the feature film ‘Miss Violence,’” he added. “I am curious to see this new version of the series and am sure it will be a success in Greece, as it was in Brazil, countries that have a lot in common.”



	

					“The Others,” courtesy of Globo
	



	The deal reinforces Globo’s positioning in the format rights market. Recently, the major banner saw a Peruvian version of “Her Own Destiny” and a Portuguese adaptation of “Her Own Destiny.”

	“The start of filming for the Greek version of ‘The Others’ is another important step in our international formats strategy,” said Angela Colla, Head of International Business at Globo. “The partnership with Alpha TV proves the strength of Brazilian narratives that transcend borders. The essence of Lucas Paraizo’s text is about human relationships, and we are excited to see how this story will resonate with the Greek audience.”

	Christos Kompos, Program Director at Alpha TV, said that their adaptation of “The Others” “underscores Alpha TV’s unwavering commitment to delivering cinematic, top-tier drama to the Greek market.”

	“Partnering with a global powerhouse like Globo gives us the creative foundation to produce something truly exceptional,” he added. “Lucas Paraizo has written a narrative that holds a direct mirror to modern society, showing how quickly community ties can fracture when people stop talking to one another. Under the visionary direction of Alexandros Avranas and led by a phenomenal ensemble cast, we are elevating this incredible Brazilian psychological drama into a culturally distinct, high-end production. It is a privilege to collaborate with Globo to breathe new life into a story that is as globally relevant as it is locally poignant.”

schema.headline: Silver Lion Winner ‘Miss Violence’ Director Alexandros Avranas to Helm Greek Adaptation of Globoplay’s Hit Series ‘The Others’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Hannah Einbinder Speaks Out After Being Arrested at Netanyahu Protest: ‘Let Us Not Mistake the Spectacle for the Story’
description: Hannah Einbinder is speaking out after being arrested earlier Thursday while protesting an appearance by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
body:
Hannah Einbinder is speaking out after being arrested earlier Thursday while protesting an appearance by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

	The “Hacks” star, who was protesting alongside Sarah Sherman, Susan Sarandon and others, posted on her Instagram story asking her followers to focus on “the devastating genocidal war Israel is waging against the people of Palestine and Southern Lebanon,” and not to “mistake the spectacle for the story.” About 100 protestors were arrested, according to the New York Times. 
	

	“If the pictures of my friends and me getting arrested in protest of Netanyahu’s shameful visit to New York draw attention to anything, let it be to the devastating genocidal war Israel is waging against the people of Palestine and Southern Lebanon — to the settler attacks, the home demolitions, the bombing of people as they sleep; to the crimes that happen every SINGLE day but garner almost no international press coverage,” Einbinder wrote. 


	“The U.S. government has the power to bring an end to all of this killing, pillaging, and land theft, yet instead it chooses to welcome the butcher of Gaza with open arms,” Einbinder continued. “The fact that the orchestrator of all this bloodshed is roaming freely in our cities is an indictment of BOTH REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS who enable and protect architects of genocide like Netanyahu. Let us not mistake the spectacle for the story: genocide is the headline, and it is time for it to end.”

	Netanyahu spoke at the U.N. General Assembly in New York and called the demonstrators “phony human rights protestors” as he asked where they were when Iranian security forces killed thousands in January.
	

	“Did you organize mass rallies, hunger strikes?” Netanyahu asked in his speech. “Did you protest outside the Iranian mission to the U.N.?”

schema.headline: Hannah Einbinder Speaks Out After Being Arrested at Netanyahu Protest: ‘Let Us Not Mistake the Spectacle for the Story’

title: Taylor Swift Still Has Unfinished Business With Her Exes — Thank God! — While Also Mooning Over Her Groom in ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’: New Tracks Review
description:
Sep 24, 2026 11:09pm PT	
	

	
		Taylor Swift Still Has Unfinished Business With Her Exes — Thank God! — While Also Mooning Over Her
body:
Sep 24, 2026 11:09pm PT	
	

	
		Taylor Swift Still Has Unfinished Business With Her Exes — Thank God! — While Also Mooning Over Her Groom in ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’: New Tracks Review
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Republic
	

		
	
				

	If you’re a Taylor Swift fan, one of your deepest fears this year might have been that the pop superstar will be so wrapped up in a long, rapturous honeymoon that she’ll neglect to bring us down by continuing to write about the bums that got away, or any lingering regrets that were accumulated on the way to the skybox. So it will come as some relief that three of the four new tracks on “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” prove she has no intention of turning in her Tortured Poets membership card any time soon.

	Meanwhile, the fourth track, “Cleveland!,” establishes that she also has no intention of stopping writing about marital bliss, in the giddiest form possible, with an unrepentant sunniness so blinding it could almost blot out the memory that she’d ever written an elegy in her life. You’ve been warned.

	However it’s packaged, these four tracks essentially constitute a new EP — something she really hasn’t formally given us since 2008’s “Beautiful Eyes” — more than they feel like any kind of obvious addendum to “The Life of a Showgirl,” despite reassembling the same trio of Avengers (Max Martin, Shellback and herself) for the task. Call if what you want: as much as the world loves Swift as the 21st century’s quintessential album artist, it’s refreshing to get something fast and easily digestible from her between pop opuses, too. Here’s how these four tracks taste at first bite:



	“Patient Zero.” When Swift thinks of a certain recent ex in her past, she does not think of Tim McGraw. She thinks of hospitals, and/or pandemics. One has to suspect that if “Patient Zero” has a real-life inspiration, it’s the same guy who inspired her to write that she was dying, emotionally, in “You’re Losing Me,” the scary post-“Midnights” bonus track that appeared to be about her longest-term relationship going into its last throes on life support. But as harrowing as “You’re Losing Me” was, “Patient Zero” is absolutely chipper, since she’s singing about being long since recovered from the malady and remembering it only for the sake of warning the fellow’s current paramour about how his good-guy act won’t be nourishing in the end.

	The sound is very different from anything on “The Life of a Showgirl,” so it makes some sense to learn that this and the other tracks were recorded after that album was already out (and very long after it was recorded). The dry drum sound heard on much of “Showgirl” is replaced here with electronic percussion, while the key bit of instrumentation is a violin, or something built to emulate one. If you didn’t know better, you might guess this was a stray Jack Antonoff track, since it doesn’t bear any of the obvious Martin/Shellback hallmarks. There’s a bittersweet, lopingly mid-tempo feel to it that we haven’t heard in, well, a fortnight.

	Fans will point to her telling the ex’s new gal that she should take the sisterly advice from “someone who had him and walked away,” which does narrow down the possibilities of who it could be about IRL, if anyone. And from that, prompt the cries of “She’s married, and she still hasn’t gotten over it?” The point is kind of that she has. But good for her for keeping that memory mill alive; she’s going to need it to keep writing songs that aren’t all white picket fences. Plus, we love a T-Swift who forgives — maybe — but never, ever forgets.





	“Cleveland!” Listen, this one is just effing goofy — calibrated somewhere between the cheeky self-celebration of “Me!” and the cheerleading of “So High School” and “Wood.” Not everyone loves Taylor Swift being a love-besotted goofball, but if that is offensive to you, modern technology makes it pretty easy to skip directly from track 1 to track 3. On first and second listen, I’m not sure whether it’s going to grow on me or gnaw at me in the future. But every singer who’s found love, especially just a bit later in life, deserves the shot at writing a honeymoon song or ten. So when it comes to the contagious ebullience here, you can consider some of us patient zero for succumbing to it.

	And this is a charmer, at least if you can buy into the notion that Swift still considers herself an underdog; it’s almost like the direct happy sequel to “You Belong With Me,” in a way. Does Swift, having been queen of the world for this many years, still think of herself as a loser who’s pulling out of here to win? Well, apparently she’s been reading the comments, and is virtually quoting them back in the verses as she refers to the school of thought that she is the world’s clumsiest dancer (hardly true, but it’s out there). And just as on “Reputation” she could not believe that her new boy at the time was willing to see past all the lies of Kanye-gate and love her anyway, here she can barely believe that Travis will not hold it against her that she is not pop’s quintessential hoofer. The woman doth protest too much about how much the internet holds against her, but anyway, she has been to Cleveland Heights now, where there are also some non-ballerinas, and made herself at home. It’s sweet.

	Musically, Martin and Shellback (and Swift herself, to offer proper co-producer credit) are switching it up again here, with some very live-sounding drum rolls here, in contrast to the electronic rhythms of “Patient Zero.” But floating above those drums is a keyboard line that sounds right out of the synth-pop late ’80s… although A Flock of Seagulls or their ilk would never have gotten prosaic enough to offer a spoken monologue like: “You only need to find one person in this entire world who doesn’t find you completely insufferable, and I have an important announcement to make — I found mine.” 

	(Now, will we get an exclamatory “Florida!!!”/”Cleveland!” mashup at some point on the next tour?)





	“Pink Clouding.” We’re all going to agree that this presents itself as the finest of the four on first blush, right? (Although it’s pretty close to a tie between the final two.) The lush, overdubbed vocals that herald the dawning of the track, followed by a steady pulse and cheerfully boomy undercurrents, make this sound like it could have been on “Lover” or, yes, even a “1989” outtake. It’s one of Swift’s regret tracks, in the lineage that stretches back to the more somber “Back to December,” a done-somebody-wrong number in which the singer sounds wistful about the boy she ghosted, disappearing from a cloud they were mutually enjoying. 

	One recovery center defines “pink cloud syndrome” as “a temporary phase of intense euphoria, optimism and overconfidence experienced during the early stages of addiction recovery.” In other words, maybe the pink cloud she hopped onto with the guy in question was… a getaway car. Anyway, euphoria is something some Swifties may experience with this one on repeat, even if it means to be a cautionary tale. A

	nd all this time later into her career, with the stereotype that she writes primarily vindictively still refusing to die in some circles, it’s still disarming to hear her put her guard down and confess: “Neither of us knew at the time that I was a liar… Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry…. I wake up scared that I left scars on a good person.” Nobody needs to worry that all that time spent screaming over touchdowns and penalties has knocked the shockingly tender poetry out of her.





	“Babylon.” The most lyrically elusive song of the fresh quartet, “Babylon” is as mysterious as “Cleveland!” is determinedly simple. Is Babylon anything like Wonderland? (And to quote one instant tweet that popped up from a literalist within minutes of the song going live: “Who the hell is Aunt Virginia?”) It gets back to her roots right at the top with an acoustic guitar that briefly seems to place it in Aaron Dessner territory… or maybe the real backdating should be to “White Horse,” since Swift seems to be referencing it when she writes, “That small town’s even smaller now in your rear view,” a pretty clear callback.) Again, the sound is fuller here, more suggestive and resonant, than on most of the dialed-down original “Showgirl” tracks. 

	What it means is difficult to parse right in the moment, but there are sone superior lines to pick out: “You ran with all the wild things / A liberated libertine who longed for home.” Is that Swift talking about herself in her immediate pre-Travis days, when she was running with one hell of a seeming wild thing? “Love is ice upon the ladder that you need to climb” is a whoa moment. And she hasn’t written many better one-liners than: “The self-harm of never being where you are.” It sounds most like a song of empathy, maybe partly directed at herself but more apparently written in a loving manner for an ex she once would have killed with a thousand cuts but now has some real sympathy for. We can appreciate that it’s “Cleveland!” that gives her life, but part of her heart is still with the ones in Babylon, a path not taken on the way to MSG.

title: Paramount’s David Ellison Attends Trump White House State Dinner for Chinese President; CNN and MS NOW Reporters Barred From Event
description:
Sep 24, 2026 8:53pm PT	
	

	
		Paramount’s David Ellison Attends Trump White House State Dinner for Chinese President; CNN and MS NO
body:
Sep 24, 2026 8:53pm PT	
	

	
		Paramount’s David Ellison Attends Trump White House State Dinner for Chinese President; CNN and MS NOW Reporters Barred From Event
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Getty Images
	

		
	
				
	David Ellison, CEO of Paramount Skydance, dined at the White House Thursday evening at the state dinner held for visiting Chinese President Xi Jinping — but the White House shut out reporters for CNN, the Warner Bros. Discovery-owned news network Ellison is on the cusp of gaining control over, as well as MS NOW.

	Ellison attended the soiree with his wife, Sandra Lynn Ellison, among a guest list of more than 100 government officials and business execs. Ellison’s Paramount is coming down the home stretch in closing a $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros., after reaching a settlement with 12 Democratic state attorneys general this week. (The judge in the case is still reviewing the proposed settlement, which does not require major concessions from Paramount.) The Paramount-WBD deal was approved by Trump’s Justice Department earlier this year without any conditions.
	

	Also attending the state dinner were tech bigwigs including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Apple chairman Tim Cook, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta chairman and CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Microsoft chairman and CEO Satya Nadella, and Elon Musk.


	Other guests included Fox News’ Bret Baier, Laura Ingraham and Jesse Watters; Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy and his wife, Cheryl Hines; and U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts and his wife, Jane Sullivan Roberts.

	According to CNN, the White House denied two of its staffers from covering Xi’s arrival back at the White House for the dinner after “trying to tell the network which type of journalists could cover the event.” A “press wrangler” barred a CNN producer and reporter from accessing the event and “told them to ‘talk to’ White House Communications Director Steven Cheung,” CNN reported. Staffers from MS NOW also were prevented from covering the Chinese president’s arrival.
	

	The White House’s blocking of CNN and MS NOW from covering the state dinner came after Donald Trump banned the networks (and Politico) from White House events. The news outlets sued, and a judge granted a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore their access. The White House complied and reissued press passes to staffers for the outlets Thursday morning — but then denied the networks the ability to cover the dinner.

	Trump is known to be friendly with both David Ellison and his father, Oracle founder and mega-billionaire Larry Ellison. This April, David Ellison in threw a dinner party in Washington, D.C., “honoring” Trump and the First Amendment, which was attended by CBS News execs and journalists.

	On the menu for Thursday’s dinner, per the White House: A first course of a “silky-smooth velouté” made of sweet yellow squash, followed by sesame-crusted sea bass, accompanied by braised baby bok choy and roasted garden eggplant. For dessert was a “smooth vanilla crémeux” with a “vibrant sour cherry confit center” atop a “rich walnut frangipane,” and ice cream made with “harvested White House honey.”

	Performances during the dinner were headlined by Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at Trump’s 2025 presidential inauguration, along with military musicians from the U.S. Marines Corps and the U.S. Army.

title: Gaussian Scout, Pixentinel Take Top Prizes at San Sebastián’s Zinemaldia Startup Challenge
description: SAN SEBASTIÁN, Spain — Finland’s Gaussian Scout (formerly listed Virtual Location Scouting) and Spain’s Pixentinel claimed the top prizes at the 202
body:
SAN SEBASTIÁN, Spain — Finland’s Gaussian Scout (formerly listed Virtual Location Scouting) and Spain’s Pixentinel claimed the top prizes at the 2026 Zinemaldia Startup Challenge, the San Sebastián Festival’s flagship technology competition.

	Gaussian Scout, a browser-based virtual location scouting platform being developed by Finnish cinematographer Antti Ahokoivu, won Best European Project with its €10,000  and also picked up the €3,000 Special Mention for Entrepreneurship. Spanish streaming-operations startup Pixentinel took the €30,000 Best Spanish Project award. Rather than simply flagging when a live stream has broken, Pixentinel aims to determine where a failure originated supplu evidence to the diagnosis and, where possible, automatically trigger a response. The proposition is aimed at broadcasters and streaming operators feel the hit of short interruptions during live programming can become lost viewers and revenue.
	

	Ahokoivu admitted the double win came as a surprise after travelling from Finland with a project that is still pre-commercial somewhat a side project to his Cinematorgraphy work. More important than the prize itself, he said, was seeing people engage with the idea. “People come to talk and are interested about it,” he told Variety. “You get more confident that there is something interesting.”


	The technology grew directly out of Ahokoivu’s work as a cinematographer and his experience trying to get different departments to understand a location in the same way before a shoot. “Having some tools that you can visualise things with, that you talk about the same things, what we’re going to do, helps so much,” he said. The prize money will now help Gaussian Scout move into tests on real productions and further develop the cloud-based system that will eventually allow users to upload and work with their own digital twins.
	

	The 2026 Zinemaldia Startup Challenge offered €30,000 for the Best Spanish Project, €10,000 for the Best European Project and a €3,000 Special Mention for Entrepreneurship. The competition is the centerpiece of the Festival’s Zinemaldia & Technology initiative and is organized by the San Sebastián Festival in collaboration with Tecnalia, ALÍA and Vicomtech.

	The Spanish competition also forms part of Spanish Screenings: Financing & Tech, supported by Spain’s Ministry of Culture through ICAA, the Ministry for Digital Transformation and Civil Service, ICEX, the Málaga Festival and the San Sebastián Festival. Prior to the win announcement the ten finalists, five Spanish and five from elsewhere in Europe, pitched their projects with each given a strict 10 minutes to present and field questions.

	We profile the companies below:
	
		European Finalists	
	
		GaussianScout (Virtual Location Scouting Finland)	

	Cinematographer Antti Ahokoivu is developing this browser-based tool intended to make remote location scouting more spatially informative than conventional photographs. Ahokoivu’s starting insight was simple: flat images rarely communicate the true proportions and geometry of a filming location for the disparate teams. GaussianScout, formerly listed as Virtual Location Scouting, brings Gaussian splats, XGRIDS scans, photogrammetry and related 3D capture methods into a shared environment where filmmakers can explore spaces, frame potential shots, even measure spaces accurately. Script-import tools are also planned. The project is still pre-commercial, with a subscription launch is targeted for autumn 2027.
	
		Graphrs (Germany)	

	Berlin-based Graphrs wants to become the “operating system for video production,” orchestrating everything from scheduling and staffing to shoots and AI-assisted content creation in a single platform. Co-founder and CEO Thomas Brömme pitched the product as infrastructure for companies producing video repeatedly across multiple markets, currently backed by a network of around 20 camera teams. Brömme cited names including TikTok, UNIQLO and the WHO as examples of its client base.
	
		SuperScout (United Kingdom)	

	SuperScout, founded by Gabriel Isserlis, turns filmmakers’ accumulated location research into private, searchable, map-based databases. Isserlis gave the example of working alongside a Disney location scout and seeing how painful it was to retrieve alternatives when a booked location suddenly became unavailable and showing how this scout was able to find an alternative location scouted 6 years prior quickly and getting the production day back on track. The platform stores previous scouts, imagery and location data so teams can find options instead of starting again. At Zinemaldia, SuperScout said it was being used across 14 countries, including by the BBC, and that 11 customers had also invested in the company. English Heritage is a confirmed institutional customer.
	
	
		TheGreenShot (Belgium)	

	Belgium’s TheGreenShot automates sustainability measurement and carbon reporting for film, television and other entertainment productions. Co-founder Max Hermans described the opportunity as replacing today’s scattered spreadsheets with software able to ingest accounting, supplier, expense and on-set data and turn it into customised reporting at scale. The pitch argued that its advantage over horizontal carbon platforms such as Greenly or Watershed is deep entertainment-industry specificity. Its public customer roster includes HBO, Chanel and Banijay, while Hermans announced Fremantle as a new customer during the Zinemaldia pitch.
	
		THELMA (Finland)	

	Finnish startup THELMA is building an identity-protection service for actors, influencers and other public figures whose image, voice or likeness may be impersonated or reused without permission online. Founder Aleksi Hyvärinen described a workflow of finding suspected misuse, preserving evidence, helping initiate action and then reporting outcomes back to the customer. The business is already testing a subscription model, with pitch pricing of roughly €350 per month for individuals and €499 for agencies.
	
		Spanish Finalists	
	
		Volum (Spain)	

	Barcelona-based Volum Technologies is commercialising years of i2CAT research into real-time volumetric communication. Its HoloMIT technology captures, compresses, streams and renders people as live 3D representations, allowing remote participants to appear “there” rather than as flat video, as long as you don a headset of course. The company spun out of i2CAT in 2025 following more than €3.7 million of research investment and is now developing an ecosystem spanning an SDK and products such as HoloBooth and HoloTotem. Volum’s broader ambition is to make holographic presence as accessible as videoconferencing, using relatively standard cameras rather than specialised studio-scale capture infrastructure.
	
		Pixentinel (Spain)	

	Pixentinel is developing an operational-intelligence layer for live streaming that, it was proposed, goes beyond detecting outages to diagnosing their likely cause and automatically triggering responses. Its system analyses video signals in context, attaches evidence and confidence scores to detected problems and can activate webhooks when intervention is required. The pitch is aimed at broadcasters, streaming platforms and telecom operators whose existing monitoring stacks generate fragmented alerts that engineers must manually correlate and react to. Pixentinel’s core proposition is therefore reducing the time between a streaming failure starting and an operations team understanding and deploying a fix for it.
	
	
		intoreality.tv (Spain)	

	Barcelona-based Into Reality offers a white-label immersive streaming platform that lets traditional 2D feeds coexist with VR180 and VR360 video. Viewers can switch cameras, audio streams and perspectives across phones, computers, tablets and VR headsets, effectively becoming their own live-event director. The platform can be embedded into a customer’s website or deployed as a standalone audiovisual service, with AVOD, subscription and pay-per-view monetisation models. Into Reality has also licensed i2CAT’s Sync-X technology, expanding its ability to deliver synchronised multicamera and multiscreen experiences for entertainment, culture, sport and live events.
	
		HaMo Real-Time Animation System (Spain)	

	HaMo Animation is building patented hardware and software for animating digital characters live, combining the responsiveness of traditional puppetry with real-time virtual production. HaMo showed the technology works with 2D, 3D, realistic and stylised characters and has already been used for promotional content around “Tad and the Magic Lamp” enabling the IP to be used live in front of Spanish distributors. The stated ambition is to productise and sell the hardware, with consumer applications potentially following in the future. José Luis Farías demonstrated the system live arguing that speed and production cost distinguish it from AI-generated animation workflows starting to appear. 
	
		Dymensium (Spain)	

	Valencia-based Dymensium is developing a volumetric-capture pipeline built around Gaussian Splatting, particularly 4DGS for moving subjects. Founder Jacinto Nicolás framed the pitch around the rapid evolution from NeRFs to Gaussian techniques and a workflow spanning capture, Gaussian generation, cleaning and integration. Its studio uses 120 synchronised cameras and targets film, VFX, games and immersive media, where directors can reposition the virtual camera after capture. Dymensium also pointed to Gaussian Splatting’s emerging use in major film production namely in James Gunn’s “Superman” as evidence that the underlying technology is moving into commercial workflows.

title: Aamir Khan to Receive Screen Icon Award as Singapore Film Festival Opens With Hur Jin-ho’s ‘The Assassin(s)’
description: The Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) will present its Screen Icon Award to Indian actor, director and producer Aamir Khan at its 37th e
body:
The Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) will present its Screen Icon Award to Indian actor, director and producer Aamir Khan at its 37th edition, with a 25th-anniversary Special Presentation screening of “Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India” alongside director Ashutosh Gowariker. 

	The festival opens with South Korean thriller “The Assassin(s),” directed by Hur Jin-ho and starring Yoo Hae-jin, Park Hae-il and Lee Min-ho. Hur and supporting cast members Shim Eun-kyung and Park Sung-hoon will attend the opening.
	

	As previously announced, SGIFF will give its Cinema Honorary Award, the festival’s top prize for lasting contributions to Asian cinema, to Japanese filmmaker Kore-eda Hirokazu, with his film “Look Back” screening as part of the program.


	SGIFF executive director Jeremy Chua said the edition brings some of the most respected talents and consequential work being made across Asia to Singapore. “Around it, we have also reconsidered how audiences encounter a festival with new presentation formats and points of entry, a ticketing platform that is markedly more intuitive, an industry programme expanded into a resource centre for artists, technicians and storytellers at every stage of practice, and a new free-to-attend section at the intersection of creativity and technology, attending to the forms storytelling will take next,” Chua said.

	SGIFF’s “In Conversation With” dialogue series will also feature Shim Eun-kyung, filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun and Hong Kong actor Anthony Wong, who will take part in a post-screening dialogue tied to his first acting role in “My Name Ain’t Suzie.” Korean New Wave director Yim Soon-rye will serve as jury head of the Asian Feature Film Competition, while Fukada Koji, director of “Nagi Notes,” cinematographers Ashizawa Akiko and Tom Harari, and director Jacob Cheung will also take part in the festival.
	

	The lineup spotlights more than 25 Singapore productions and co-productions that have earned recognition at festivals including Cannes, Sundance, Toronto, Venice and Melbourne. Among them, “Ah Girl” star Ong Xuan Jing won best actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival’s Young Cinema Competition, while director Ang Geck Geck won the Youth Jury Award at the International Film Festival Rotterdam. Nelson Yeo’s “The House on the Moon” premiered in competition at Locarno, and Tan Si En of Momo Film Co. co-produced “Nagi Notes,” which premiered in competition at Cannes. Daniel Hui edited “Sleep No More” and “The Burning Giants,” which premiered at the Berlin and Venice film festivals, respectively. Anthony Chen of Giraffe Pictures co-produced “Four Seasons in Java,” and Lai Weijie of E&W Films co-produced “9 Temples to Heaven,” which premiered in the Directors’ Fortnight at Cannes.

	SGIFF program director Thong Kay Wee said, “Singapore’s film industry is enjoying its hard-earned recognition on the world stage. This year’s selection of Singapore films and co-productions reflects an increasingly diverse creative ecosystem that is producing internationally competitive work. We are proud to share that many of these filmmakers found their first mentorships through SGIFF, so sharing their stories and work on Singapore screens this year is, in that sense, a homecoming.”

	The SGIFF Film Fund also returns after a hiatus. The Tan Ean Kiam Foundation, previously a backer of the Southeast Asian Documentary Grant, will now also support the Southeast Asian Short Film Grant, with both programs falling under the Tan Ean Kiam Foundation-SGIFF banner as SEA-Doc and SEA-Shorts. SEA-Doc shifts this cycle to backing feature documentaries in late edit or finishing stages, while SEA-Shorts continues supporting emerging Southeast Asian filmmakers. The open call for both grants runs Nov. 5 to Dec. 5.

	The festival will introduce a Junior Explorers section with sensory-friendly screenings for younger audiences, opening with stop-motion feature “Brave Cat.” Its Undercurrent section will open with three live performances: Taiwanese puppetry piece “Corporeal Forms: Four Stories,” live video gaming work “The Compression Zone” and analog film and music performance “Imagination + The Rest Is My Ghost.” SGIFF Pro, the festival’s industry arm, adds three new programs this year: Parallax, a free public program on filmmaking and immersive technology; Off Campus, a student initiative connecting classroom training with industry exposure; and the Pitching Forum, aimed at co-production between Singapore and international partners.
	

	The festival, supported by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), runs Oct. 21 to Nov. 1.

title: The Horror Show Launches at Academy Museum: Costumes and Props From ‘Halloween,’ ‘Saw,’ ‘Poltergeist’ and More
description: Just in time for the scariest season, the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles is unveiling The Horror Show, a major survey of costumes, p
body:
Just in time for the scariest season, the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles is unveiling The Horror Show, a major survey of costumes, props, drawings, posters and other artifacts from the most iconic horror films throughout the history of cinema. The exhibit opens Saturday.
From Bela Lugosi’s original cape from the 1931 “Dracula” to Aunt Gladys’ pantsuit from “Weapons,” the exhibit showcases classic and lesser-known films from every era. Beloved characters like Freddy Krueger, Michael Myers and Chucky are represented along with more recent titles such as “Sinners,” “Get Out,” “Midsommar” and “The Babadook.”
“Many different types of films can be considered horror filmmaking, from vampires to slashers to thrillers,” said Academy museum director Amy Homma as she introduced the exhibit Thursday. “Horror has its own filmic history, it’s own origins through literature, culture and art and its own lineage.”
“The Horror Show revolves around a simple question: Why do horror films mean so much to so many people?” said the exhibit’s curator Jessica Niebel. “Horror reflects the anxieties of its time, but it also gives us a safe space to confront those anxieties, to look at the things that frighten us and that we desire.”
The exhibit’s chambers feature themes like slashers, religion, ghosts and science, with several interactive photo ops from a coffin to a chance for a selfie with Mrs. Bates from “Psycho,” and guests exit through an eerie blood room. If that’s all a little too scary for the younger visitors to the museum, an accompanying exhibit called Zombies! goes easier on the gore.
The Academy will screen a robust schedule of horror films to complement the exhibit, kicking off with an appearance by Jamie Lee Curtis and John Carpenter for “Halloween” and a Carpenter retrospective.
The Horror Show will run through July 25, 2027.

title: 4-Year-Old Girl Dies After Being Found in Trash Can Full of Water
description:
4-Year-Old Girl
                          Dies After Parents Find Her in Trash Can Full of Water
body:
4-Year-Old Girl
                          Dies After Parents Find Her in Trash Can Full of Water
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 24, 2026
                            6:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Authorities are investigating the death of 4-year-old Jayde Wooten who was found upside down in a trash can full of water and fish.
      
    
            According to WGXA, the girl's father told a deputy that he'd just gotten home and couldn't find his daughter in her room.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He says he then woke up Jayde's mother, who claims to have fallen asleep while Jayde was eating in the kitchen.
      

            The outlet reports that the father said he was "frantically" searching for Jayde when he heard her mother scream.
      
    
            He says when he ran back inside, he found Jayde in a bathroom, upside down in a trash can that had been filled with water and fish.
      
    
            The father carried Jayde outside, where neighbors attempted to perform CPR on the child.
      
    
            According to the Bibb County Sheriff’s Office, Jayde was taken to a local medical facility, where she was pronounced dead. BSO says they're investigating the incident.
      
    
            A GoFundMe has been created to help the parents cover funeral costs and support them as they grieve this terrible tragedy.

title: Nolan Wells District Attorney Slams Ben Crump Over Alleged Cell Phone Evidence
description:
Nolan Wells' District Attorney
                          Slams Ben Crump Over Alleged Cell Phone
body:
Nolan Wells' District Attorney
                          Slams Ben Crump Over Alleged Cell Phone Evidence
                          'Stop Playing Games!!!'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 24, 2026
                            7:47 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The District Attorney who investigated Nolan Wells' death fired back at the late teen’s family lawyer Ben Crump ... hours after he held a press conference with alleged new evidence.
      
    
            Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath criticized Crump's claims Thursday that texts were deleted on Nolan's phone.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Crump and a forensic expert his team hired said they discovered data had been deleted from the phone. They said the missing messages were on Snapchat.
      
    
            McLlrath said, "The user action discussed by [Crump's team] is from other snapchat users, not someone physically accessing Nolan Wells' phone."
      
    
            She added, "If the Crump team has evidence to the contrary, they have not provided it to us. The Grand Jury report outlined the other evidence they received, including cell phone downloads, surveillance data, GPS data, and the printed report of Nolan’s cell phone."
      
    
            She ended with another dig at Crump ... writing if his team "genuinely has new information or evidence that Nolan Wells was murdered they should stop playing games and immediately provide it to me."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Nolan disappeared July 4 during a boat outing with Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour. His body was found two days later. After reviewing testimony from 43 witnesses, cellphone downloads, GPS data, surveillance footage and more, a grand jury returned a "no true bill" ... meaning no charges were filed. The panel said the circumstances were consistent with drowning, but Nolan's official cause and manner of death remain undetermined.

title: Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror to Return to Work in A Week
description:
Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror
                          Clocking Back Into Work
body:
Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror
                          Clocking Back Into Work
                          ... After Bombshell Mistrial
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 25, 2026
                            12:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After a media whirlwind, the holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is ready to get back to work and business as usual, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Michael Desronvil's lawyer, Edward Andrew Paltzik, tells TMZ ... Michael's been "laying low" since the mistrial.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            He tells us the property maintenance company he works for has been very supportive during this "challenging time."
      

            Paltzik tells us Michael had been taking time off work, but plans to get back to the grind in a week.
      
    
            He says Michael's been "processing everything" and spending his time going to church, reading and hanging with his girlfriend ... but he's ready to get back to "normalcy."
      
    
            Paltzik tells TMZ ... "He wants to eventually tell his story, but for right now he has no plans to speak publicly ... because it’s been a lot."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The lawyer continued ... "He’s incredibly grateful and touched by everyone that has supported him and donated."
      
    
            According to Paltzik, they've been in touch with Massachusetts State Police and the District Attorney regarding Michael's safety.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we previously reported, Michael's planning to file a bar complaint against Lindsay's lawyer, Kevin Reddington.
      
    
            Sources say Michael felt targeted in the days after the trial and is calling for Reddington to be suspended or disbarred.

title: Cops Called On Kim Zolciak's Son After Allegedly Shooting Pellets Toward Horses
description:
Kim Zolciak
                          Cops Called On Son After Allegedly Shooting Pellets
body:
Kim Zolciak
                          Cops Called On Son After Allegedly Shooting Pellets
                          To Scare Horses
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                September 24, 2026
                
                            4:15 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 24, 2026
                                5:55 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            More drama involving Kim Zolciak's kids ... one of her sons was accused of shooting a pellet gun to scare a neighbor's horses ... and the cops were called.
      
    
            TMZ obtained a police report, dated July 14, 2026, in which cops were called out to the Equestrian Reserve across the street from the 'RHOA' alum's home in Alpharetta, Georgia.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The employee at the equestrian ranch told cops she believed one of Kim's kids had been shooting pellets from a pellet gun from his home onto her property. She said, to her knowledge, no horses or individuals had been struck by the pellets, but she said she believed the kid was shooting toward the facility to frighten the horses.
      

            The employee said they could not provide a detailed description of the kid, and the name of the juvenile is redacted in the report.
      
    
            The officer who arrived said they saw 20 to 30 pellets scattered in the roadway next to the property.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            The equestrian ranch employee said they had prior issues with the kids ... claiming fireworks had been discharged from the home in the past and saying the kids had been "verbally rude and uncooperative" when confronted about the behavior.
      
    
            The cops say they knocked on Kim's door, and two young boys answered, but only one was Kim's son. Cops say the kid admitted shooting the pellet gun but denied he was trying to hit horses or people.
      
    
            The cops did not make any arrests, and no charges were filed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Kim's family is going through it at the moment … with her son Kroy Jr. recently being released from jail after being accused of sexual assault on a schoolmate.
      
    
            Kroy Jr. is currently being prosecuted as an adult.
